title: Because this story did not begin with Abishag.
paragraphs: Because this story did not begin with Abishag.
It did not begin with Adonijah.
And it certainly did not begin with Solomon's anger.
It began long before that, when a king looked from his rooftop and made a decision that would leave scars across generations.
His name was David.
And the woman at the center of that earlier scandal was Bathsheba.
The same Bathsheba who would one day walk into Solomon's throne room.
The same Bathsheba whose life had been shattered by royal power.
The same Bathsheba whose son now sat upon Israel's throne.
And the same Bathsheba who was about to discover that even a mother's request could carry consequences she never anticipated.
Stay with this story.
Because somewhere between David's rooftop, Solomon's throne, and the cross of Jesus Christ, Scripture confronts a question we would rather avoid.
What happens when something we desperately want begins to matter more to us than what God has already made clear?
Bathsheba knew what it meant to live beneath the weight of another person's desire.

Second Samuel 11 tells us that David saw her bathing, sent messengers, and took her. The biblical account places responsibility upon David, the king who possessed the power and initiated the encounter.
Bathsheba was married to Uriah, a soldier serving David's kingdom.
When she became pregnant, David attempted to conceal what had happened.
When his attempts failed, he arranged for Uriah to be placed in a deadly military position and abandoned in battle.
Uriah died.
Bathsheba mourned her husband.
And David took her into his house.
For a season, the scandal may have appeared buried beneath the authority of a royal throne.
But God had seen everything.
Second Samuel 11:27 declares:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” (KJV)
That sentence should terrify anyone who believes that successfully hiding sin means escaping God's attention.
David could manipulate military orders.
He could command messengers.
He could control appearances.
But he could not control the holiness of God.
When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
And Nathan announced that the LORD had put away his sin.
Yet forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
The child born from that first pregnancy died. Violence and betrayal would trouble David's household. His family would experience devastating conflict.
We must be careful here. Scripture does not permit us to blame Bathsheba for David's abuse of royal power, nor does it teach that every suffering person is being punished for a particular sin.
But it does reveal something deeply sobering.
Sin can be forgiven without becoming harmless.
And choices made in secret can leave consequences that outlive the moment.
Still, the story did not end in disgrace.
Bathsheba later bore Solomon.
Second Samuel 12:24 says that the LORD loved him.
Think about that.
Out of a family history marked by grief and moral failure, God continued His redemptive purposes.
Not because David's wrongdoing was acceptable.
Not because Bathsheba's suffering was insignificant.
But because human sin does not possess the final authority over God's mercy.
Grace does not rename evil as good. Grace reveals that evil does not have the power to defeat God's ultimate purpose.
Years passed.
David grew old.
And the question of who would inherit his throne became increasingly urgent.
Adonijah, another son of David, decided to make himself king.
First Kings 1:5 records his declaration:
“I will be king.” (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not, “Has the LORD appointed me?”
Not, “What is my father's instruction?”
Not, “How can I serve God's people?”
Simply:
“I will be king.”
Adonijah gathered supporters, including Joab and Abiathar. He arranged a royal celebration and acted as though the kingdom already belonged to him.
But David had designated Solomon as his successor.
Through the intervention of Nathan and Bathsheba, David publicly confirmed Solomon's kingship.
Adonijah's attempted seizure of the throne collapsed.
And for a moment, it appeared that mercy might prevail.
Adonijah feared Solomon and sought refuge by grasping the horns of the altar.
Solomon did not immediately execute him.
Instead, he granted conditional mercy.
First Kings 1:52 records Solomon's warning:
“If he will shew himself a worthy man, there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth: but if wickedness shall be found in him, he shall die.” (KJV)
Adonijah had been given an opportunity to live peacefully under the king God had appointed.
That detail matters.
Because when we reach the next chapter, we are not watching an innocent man encounter a king who has never shown him mercy.
We are watching a previously defeated claimant approach the boundaries of that mercy.
And what he does next changes everything.
Adonijah approaches Bathsheba.
Imagine the tension.
She is the mother of Solomon.
He is Solomon's older half brother.
They belong to the same fractured royal family.
And Adonijah has already attempted to take the throne now occupied by her son.
When Bathsheba sees him, she asks a revealing question:
“Comest thou peaceably?” (1 Kings 2:13, KJV)
He answers:
“Peaceably.”
Then he begins speaking about the kingdom.
He tells her that the throne had been his expectation and that Israel had looked toward him as king.
But he acknowledges that the kingdom has become Solomon's, saying:
“For it was his from the LORD.” (1 Kings 2:15, KJV)
Read that carefully.
Adonijah acknowledges that Solomon's kingship came from the LORD.
Yet he is about to request something Solomon will interpret as another attempt to claim royal standing.
There is a dangerous contradiction here.
A person can acknowledge God's decision with his lips while still pursuing something that challenges it.
We cannot see every hidden thought in Adonijah's heart. Scripture does not give us permission to claim that we know every private motive.
But it does show us his previous rebellion, his present request, and Solomon's interpretation of its political meaning.
Then Adonijah says:
“Ask on my behalf for Abishag the Shunammite to be given to me as my wife.” (1 Kings 2:17, translated from the Hebrew)
Abishag.
A name that might seem insignificant to a modern reader.
But in the royal household of ancient Israel, this was no ordinary marriage proposal.
Abishag had been brought to care for the elderly David during his final days.
First Kings 1:4 explicitly states that David did not have sexual relations with her.
She was not described as David's wife in that passage, and we should not invent a marriage the text does not establish.
Nevertheless, she had occupied an intimate position within the former king's household.
In the political world of ancient monarchy, relationships involving women associated with a previous king could carry implications of succession and royal authority.
Second Samuel 16:21–22 had already demonstrated how publicly taking possession of a king's concubines could serve as a claim to his royal position.
Adonijah's request therefore carried implications far beyond romance.
Whether he personally understood every consequence or not, Solomon certainly recognized the danger.
And Bathsheba agreed to carry the request.
First Kings 2:18 records her answer:
“Well; I will speak for thee unto the king.” (KJV)
That single sentence changed the direction of the story.
Bathsheba went to Solomon.
And what happened next is one of the most striking scenes in the chapter.
When Solomon saw his mother, he rose to meet her.
He bowed before her.
Then he sat upon his throne and ordered another seat to be placed for her at his right hand.
Imagine that scene.
The most powerful man in Israel standing in honor of his mother.
The king bowing before the woman who had once endured terrible suffering under the power of another king.
Bathsheba was no longer standing at the margins of royal life.
She was seated beside her son.
Honored.
Heard.
Given a place of dignity.
And Solomon invited her to speak.
She said:
“I desire one small petition of thee; I pray thee, say me not nay.” (1 Kings 2:20, KJV)
One small petition.
That is how she described it.
Solomon answered:
“Ask on, my mother: for I will not say thee nay.”
Then Bathsheba presented the request.
Give Abishag the Shunammite to Adonijah as his wife.
And suddenly the atmosphere changed.
The king who had risen to honor his mother now responded with unmistakable alarm.
“And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also.” (1 Kings 2:22, KJV)
There it is.
The sentence that reveals why Solomon considered the request so dangerous.
In his judgment, asking for Abishag was not merely asking for a marriage.
It was effectively asking for the kingdom.
Solomon explicitly connected Adonijah's request with his status as the older brother and with the political influence of Abiathar and Joab.
To Solomon, this was a threat to the established throne.
And he refused it.
Now consider the Hebrew wording behind the confrontation.
In 1 Kings 2:22, Solomon says:
וְלָמָּה אַתְּ שֹׁאֶלֶת אֶת־אֲבִישַׁג הַשֻּׁנַמִּית לַאֲדֹנִיָּהוּ
Ve-lammah att sho'elet et-Avishag ha-Shunammit la-Adoniyyahu?
A close translation is:
“And why are you asking for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah?”
Then comes the piercing command:
וְשַׁאֲלִי־לוֹ אֶת־הַמְּלוּכָה
Ve-sha'ali lo et-ha-melukhah.
“Ask for him the kingdom also.”
The Hebrew word מְלוּכָה (melukhah) refers to kingship or royal rule.
Solomon was identifying what he believed stood behind the marriage request: a renewed challenge to royal authority.
Bathsheba had described her request as small.
Solomon understood its implications as enormous.
And here is where this ancient account begins pressing into our modern lives.
How many things have we called small because we did not want to confront what they might become?
A conversation we should never have continued.
A secret attachment we insisted was innocent.
A compromise we excused because nobody seemed hurt.
A bitterness we protected because we felt justified.
A desire we refused to surrender because we had already decided we deserved it.
Not every request hides an evil intention. Not every desire is rebellion.
But Scripture repeatedly warns that our hearts require examination.
Jeremiah 17:9 speaks of the heart's capacity for deceit.
James 1:14–15 describes how desire, when it gives birth to sin, can ultimately lead to death.
And Jesus teaches that evil actions emerge from within the human heart (Mark 7:20–23).
The danger is not merely that other people may deceive us.
It is that we can become remarkably skilled at deceiving ourselves.
We can call pride conviction.
We can call jealousy discernment.
We can call revenge justice.
We can call disobedience freedom.
We can even call our refusal to surrender “waiting for God's timing.”
And sometimes, while our mouths are saying, “Lord, Your will be done,” our decisions are quietly saying, “But I still want my throne.”
That is a terrifying place to live.
Because the human heart does not need a crown to struggle with the desire to rule.
Sometimes the throne we refuse to surrender is simply control over our own lives.
Solomon's response was immediate.
He swore by the LORD that Adonijah would die because of the request.
First Kings 2:24 says:
“Adonijah shall be put to death this day.” (KJV)
Then Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada.
And Adonijah was executed.
The chapter states the outcome without softening it.
No extended farewell.
No dramatic final speech.
No invented last-minute confession.
Just the stark conclusion of a political struggle inside Israel's royal household.
We must resist the temptation to turn this into a simplistic lesson that every harsh action taken by a biblical king automatically reflects God's moral ideal.
The narrative reports Solomon's judgment and the execution. It also places these events within the establishment of his kingdom.
But the passage does not explicitly record a fresh divine command ordering this particular execution.
The Bible's historical descriptions must be interpreted carefully. Reporting an action is not always the same as commanding believers to imitate it.
Christians are not authorized by this passage to punish personal rivals, destroy those who threaten their influence, or confuse human anger with divine justice.
The deeper warning is not that we should behave like absolute monarchs.
It is that the pursuit of power, the consequences of rebellion, and the vulnerability of human hearts are profoundly serious matters.
And there is another person in this story we should not overlook.
Abishag.
The woman whose name was spoken.
The woman whose marriage was requested.
The woman whose future became entangled with royal ambition.
She is not recorded speaking in this scene.
We are not told what she wanted.
We are not told whether anyone sought her consent.
The silence of the narrative should make us cautious about romanticizing Adonijah's proposal.
Behind the political struggle was a real woman whose wishes are not preserved in the account.
And behind many human struggles for control are people who become instruments in someone else's ambitions.
That, too, is a warning.
Whenever our desires become so important that we stop seeing the dignity of others, something has gone terribly wrong.
Jesus Christ calls His followers to a different understanding of greatness.
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus contrasts rulers who exercise power over others with the servant-hearted leadership He requires of His disciples.
Then He declares:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45, KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Adonijah reached toward a throne.
Jesus willingly humbled Himself.
Human kings struggled to preserve their power.
The eternal Son of God took the form of a servant.
Earthly rulers could sentence others to death.
Jesus went to the cross to save sinners.
And this is where the story becomes more than a palace tragedy.
Because Solomon, for all his wisdom and royal authority, was not the final answer to humanity's brokenness.
He was a flawed human king.
His reign would eventually reveal serious spiritual failures of its own.
First Kings 11 records how Solomon's heart turned away from wholehearted devotion to the LORD.
Even the king who could recognize danger in another man's ambition would not remain immune to the temptations of his own heart.
That should humble every one of us.
It is possible to recognize someone else's compromise while overlooking our own.
It is possible to speak wisely and still live foolishly.
It is possible to begin with extraordinary privilege and finish with devastating disobedience.
Knowledge alone cannot redeem the human heart.
Position cannot redeem it.
Religious heritage cannot redeem it.
Even a throne connected to God's covenant promises cannot make a sinful human being righteous.
We need a greater King.
And Scripture points us to Him.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The righteous King.
The One who came not to seize what did not belong to Him, but to fulfill the Father's will.
The One who did not manipulate His way into power but humbled Himself in obedience, even to death on a cross.
Philippians 2:8 declares:
“He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” (KJV)
Consider the difference.
Adonijah said, “I will be king.”
Jesus prayed:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” (Luke 22:42, KJV)
One statement reveals the danger of self-exaltation.
The other reveals the beauty of perfect surrender.
And only one of these men could save us.
Not Adonijah.
Not Solomon.
Not David.
Only Jesus.
Because the deepest problem in this story is not simply a disputed marriage request.
It is the fallen human heart.
The heart that wants authority without submission.
Blessing without obedience.
Forgiveness without repentance.
A crown without a cross.
And if we are willing to be spiritually honest, we have all wrestled with that heart in one form or another.
Perhaps you have never tried to take a kingdom.
But have you ever tried to take control away from God?
Have you ever prayed for His guidance while secretly deciding you would only obey if His answer matched your desires?
Have you ever justified something you knew was wrong because giving it up would hurt?
Have you ever mistaken an open opportunity for divine permission?
Or have you been so wounded by what someone else did that you now struggle to believe God can write anything beautiful from your life?
That last question matters especially when we remember Bathsheba.
Her story was not simply about the sins and ambitions of kings.
It was also about a woman who experienced loss, lived through the consequences of royal wrongdoing, and later became the mother of a king.
We should never use her later position to minimize her earlier suffering.
Nor should we suggest that suffering automatically produces earthly promotion.
But her story does remind us that a person's painful past need not be the final description of their life.
And the New Testament gives us a remarkable reminder.
In Matthew 1:6, the genealogy of Jesus identifies Solomon's mother as the woman who had been Uriah's wife.
Matthew does not erase Uriah from the story.
The Gospel does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It preserves the uncomfortable history within the family line through which the Messiah came.
Why is that so powerful?
Because God's redemptive work does not depend upon rewriting the past as though sin never existed.
He tells the truth about human failure.
And then He reveals a Savior greater than that failure.
The Gospel is not that our scandals were secretly harmless. The Gospel is that Jesus Christ is mighty enough to redeem sinners without ever calling sin righteous.
That is the grace we need.
Not a religious performance.
Not a carefully edited testimony.
Not a public image designed to conceal private wounds.
We need forgiveness.
We need repentance.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need a new heart.
And Jesus does not invite us to save ourselves by becoming impressive enough.
He calls us to turn from sin and believe the Gospel.
Mark 1:15 records His words:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is turning toward God with a changed understanding of sin and a willingness to surrender to His authority.
And grace is not permission to remain enslaved to the very things Christ came to save us from.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains us to reject ungodliness and live in a manner that honors Him.
The grace of Jesus forgives.
And the grace of Jesus transforms.
Perhaps that is the message someone reading this needs most tonight.
You have been hiding.
Not necessarily from other people.
Maybe everyone thinks you are doing well.
You still attend church.
You still share Bible verses.
You still say “God is good.”
But privately, you are exhausted from negotiating with the very things God has been calling you to surrender.
There is a habit you keep defending.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ.
A secret you are afraid to confess.
Or a wound you have mistaken for your permanent identity.
And the hardest part is that you know enough Scripture to recognize the truth.
You just do not know whether you have the courage to face it.
Listen carefully.
The same Jesus who exposes sin is the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
You do not have to pretend before Him.
You do not have to manufacture a beautiful testimony.
You do not have to convince Him that your failures were smaller than they were.
Come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not an invitation to manipulate God with empty words.
It is an invitation to genuine confession grounded in the faithfulness and righteousness of God.
And if you are in Christ, your past does not get to overrule His saving work.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
What a breathtaking contrast.
In Solomon's court, Adonijah's request ended in an execution.
At Calvary, Jesus willingly endured death so that guilty sinners who trust in Him might receive forgiveness and life.
We must not pretend those two events are morally or theologically identical.
But the contrast directs our attention to the glory of Christ.
The final hope of the Christian faith is not that we find a human king powerful enough to eliminate every rival.
It is that God has given us a Savior righteous enough to defeat sin and death.
Jesus was crucified.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
His resurrection declares that death does not possess the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not merely about surviving scandals.
It is about redemption through the crucified and risen Christ.
Not because our mistakes were insignificant.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every broken relationship is automatically restored in this life.
But because Jesus Christ can forgive sin, transform lives, restore fellowship with God, and give eternal hope to those who trust Him.
And sometimes that transformation begins with the most difficult prayer a human heart can offer.
“Lord, I wanted my own way more than I wanted Yours.”
No impressive speech.
No spiritual performance.
Just surrender.
Maybe you need to pray that tonight.
Maybe you need to stop calling something harmless when your conscience has been warning you for months.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you wounded.
Maybe you need to seek help for a destructive pattern.
Maybe you need to return to Scripture instead of listening only to voices that affirm what you already want.
Maybe you need to believe that repentance is not the end of your story.
It can be the beginning of a life increasingly shaped by Christ.
And maybe someone you love is standing at that same crossroads.
A son who has drifted from faith.
A daughter who believes she has gone too far.
A husband carrying silent shame.
A wife whose heart has been crushed.
A friend who keeps smiling while privately losing hope.
Someone who has confused religious activity with actually knowing Jesus.
Someone who needs to hear that God is holy, sin is serious, and the mercy offered through Jesus Christ is real.
Do not let this message end with you.
You can simply write “No more hiding” if you are ready to bring something into the light before God.
You do not have to expose private details or explain wounds you are not ready to share.
And if you have experienced the forgiveness and restoring mercy of Jesus, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
Not as a substitute for reading Scripture, but as a reminder to return to 1 Kings 2:13–25 and examine the passage carefully for yourself.
Read the chapter.
Read what came before it.
Ask God for wisdom to distinguish your desires from His revealed will.
Because the goal is not merely to feel moved by a powerful story.
The goal is to become a faithful disciple of Jesus Christ.
And that is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We are not here simply to produce content that stirs emotion for a few minutes before disappearing into another social media feed.
Our desire is to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in biblical truth, pursue repentance, and continue following Christ when the emotional moment has passed.
Through Gospel Warrior, we want to keep bringing Scripture-centered teaching, devotionals, encouragement, discipleship resources, and honest conversations about faith to people who need them.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical nourishment accessible, including to those who cannot afford paid materials.
Think of it as an opportunity for ongoing ministry support—an offering of generosity, not a payment for God's favor.

Scripture teaches that believers may freely and willingly support Gospel ministry. First Corinthians 9:14 recognizes the legitimacy of supporting those who proclaim the Gospel, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from pressure or compulsion.
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
That matters.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and faithful service in the life He has entrusted to you.
These products are simply expressions of encouragement and ministry identity. They are not the Gospel, and buying them is not a measure of anyone's faith.
You can still be part of this mission.
Read the Word.
Pray for those who are struggling.
You can help a message travel farther without spending anything.
Sometimes a simple share becomes the doorway to a conversation about eternity.
Sometimes a thoughtful comment gives another struggling believer the courage to admit that they need prayer.
Sometimes a saved article becomes a reminder, weeks later, to open the Bible again.
We cannot promise what God will do through any particular post.
But we can be faithful with the truth we have been entrusted to share.
And that brings us back to Bathsheba.
The mother who entered a throne room.
The king who honored her.
The request that seemed small.
The danger Solomon recognized.
The execution that followed.
And the haunting question left for every reader.
What are you asking for that you have not first surrendered to God?
What desire has become so precious that you are afraid to let Scripture examine it?
What part of your life are you still trying to rule?
Because there is a King greater than Solomon.
A King who sees the heart completely.
A King who cannot be manipulated by appearances.
A King who does not need to seize a throne because all authority in heaven and on earth belongs to Him.
And that King is Jesus Christ.
He does not invite you to pretend that sin is harmless.
He invites you to repent and believe.
He does not promise that every earthly consequence will vanish.
He promises eternal life to those who believe in Him.
He does not ask you to build a throne beside His.
He calls you to follow Him.
So before you close this article, before you scroll to the next story, before another distraction fills the silence, ask yourself one final question.
Am I truly surrendering my life to Jesus, or am I still asking Him to bless the kingdom I have built for myself?
Do not answer quickly.
Let Scripture search your heart.
Let the Holy Spirit bring conviction where repentance is needed.
Let the mercy of Christ give you courage to come into the light.

And remember that the same Bible that tells the truth about David's sin, Bathsheba's suffering, Adonijah's ambition, and Solomon's judgment also reveals the coming of the Savior through David's family line.
The scandal was not erased from the record.
But neither was God's promise defeated by it.
And for every repentant sinner who places their faith in Jesus Christ, that is hope worth holding onto.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but it does not have to become the throne from which your future is ruled—Jesus Christ is a greater King than your greatest failure.
